title: Consistent views of namespaces
first_public_date_basis: Opening date of official python/peps PR whose preserved commit history contains the earliest recovered draft; commit authoring date is not asserted to be publication date.
classification_reason: A complete namespace-view subsystem spans locals(), frame.f_locals, immediate two-way state synchronization, arbitrary mapping additions, execution contexts, and C-API migration. It is not classified whole merely because an entire PEP was retrieved.
caller: Python code inspecting or modifying its active local namespace
Debuggers and other tools inspecting a Python execution frame
C extension authors obtaining a current or caller-depth frame namespace
input: An active function, class, or module frame and its local names/values
Mapping reads/writes, including arbitrary extra name/value pairs
A frame object or a caller-stack depth for the proposed C entry points
output: Live mapping views from BOTH locals() and frame.f_locals that remain synchronized with underlying variables
Writes through a namespace view visible to running code and subsequent reads
C access to the same frame-local view; safe failure of the old borrowed-reference API
limits: The earliest draft specifies live locals(); a snapshot-only locals() result conflicts with this frozen text.
Threaded code, generators, and coroutines are expressly in scope.
No numerical performance target is specified.
The first example contains nonlocal var without its enclosing context and a sys._getframe(0) pseudocode ambiguity; preserve these as draft defects, not silently repaired executable code.
Exact error-message wording is illustrative (like), not mandatory.
first_text_only_rule: Predicates and all three search strings are derived only from this fixed earliest draft. Names present only in later recovery copies do not become first-text knowledge.

whole_must.predicate: Both locals() and frame.f_locals expose a live mapping view of the relevant execution namespace; writes to either view and underlying local-variable writes are immediately visible in the other directions.

source_positions.excerpt:
This PEP proposes make the views of namespaces consistent once more.
Modifications to ``locals()`` will show in the underlying variables,
``frame.f_locals`` will be consistent with ``locals()`` and will be
consistent with the underlying variables regardless of threading or coroutines.

All writes to the ``f_locals`` mapping will be immediately visible
in the underlying variables. All changes to the underlying variables
will be immediately visible in the mapping. The ``f_locals`` is a full
mapping, and can have arbitrary key-value pairs added to it.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Within a function set x=1, retain v=locals(), assign v["x"]=2, then change x=3 and read v["x"] and frame.f_locals["x"].
whole_must.failure_condition: A view write leaves x at 1, or a later variable assignment leaves either view stale; a snapshot-only locals() implementation fails.

whole_must.predicate: Namespace access remains consistent in class and function scopes and when execution involves threads, generators, or coroutines.

source_positions.excerpt:
The current implementation has many corner cases and oddities.
Code that works around those may need to be changed.
Code that uses ``locals()`` for simple templating, or print debugging,
will continue to work correctly. Debuggers and other tools that use
``f_locals`` to modify local variables, will now work correctly,
even in the presence of threaded code, coroutines and generators.

For example::

    class C:
        x = 1
        locals()['x'] = 2
        print(x)

prints ``2``

but::

    def f():
        x = 1
        locals()['x'] = 2
        print(x)
    f()

prints ``1``

This is inconsistent, and confusing.
With this PEP both examples would print ``2``.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Apply the same existing-local mutation in an ordinary function and a suspended generator/coroutine that resumes under the supported threading model.
whole_must.failure_condition: A mapping works only in class scope, or changes disappear when the function/generator/coroutine resumes.

whole_must.predicate: The view implements the stated mapping interface and retains arbitrary extra key/value pairs; the first-text example also expects its inserted name to be usable rather than lost.

source_positions.excerpt:
``frame.f_locals`` will return a view object on the frame that
implements the ``collections.abc.Mapping`` interface.

``locals()`` will be defined simply as::

    def locals():
        return sys._getframe(0).f_locals


All writes to the ``f_locals`` mapping will be immediately visible
in the underlying variables. All changes to the underlying variables
will be immediately visible in the mapping. The ``f_locals`` is a full
mapping, and can have arbitrary key-value pairs added to it.

For example::

    def test():
        nonlocal var
        x = 1
        locals()['x'] = 2
        locals()['y'] = 4
        locals()['z'] = 5
        y
        print(dict(locals()), x)

``test()`` will print ``{'x': 2, 'y': 4, 'z': 5} 2``

In 3.10, the above will fail with a ``NameError`` as ``y`` 
as the definition ``locals()['y'] = 4`` is lost.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Add x=2, y=4, z=5 through the live namespace view, then enumerate it and exercise the example’s subsequent y access.
whole_must.failure_condition: Keys vanish on refresh/resumption or the asserted name-access behavior is absent. The malformed nonlocal example makes literal execution unresolved; do not call it verified by silently repairing the draft.

whole_must.predicate: The C interface provides the equivalent of PyEval_Locals(int depth) for the selected stack depth and PyFrame_GetLocals(frame) for an explicit frame.

source_positions.excerpt:
C-API
-----

Two new C-API functions will be added::

    PyObject *PyEval_Locals(int depth)
    PyObject *PyFrame_GetLocals(PyFrameObject *f)

``PyEval_Locals(depth)`` is equivalent to: ``sys._getframe(depth).f_locals``
``PyFrame_GetLocals(f)`` is equivalent to: ``f.f_locals``

whole_must.falsifying_input: From nested callers request depth 0 and depth 1, and separately request an explicit suspended frame.
whole_must.failure_condition: Only the current C function’s own namespace is returned regardless of depth, or the explicit frame returns an unrelated/cached dictionary.

whole_must.predicate: The old PyEval_GetLocals() path raises an exception indicating that the unsafe borrowed-reference interface must be replaced.

source_positions.excerpt:
The existing  C-API function ``PyEval_GetLocals()`` will always raise an
exception with a message like::

    PyEval_GetLocals() is unsafe. Please use PyEval_Locals() instead.

This is necessary as ``PyEval_GetLocals()`` 
returns a borrowed reference which cannot be made safe.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Call the old PyEval_GetLocals() in an otherwise valid active frame.
whole_must.failure_condition: It silently returns the old borrowed dictionary rather than raising as the draft requires.

whole_must.predicate: Repeated views over an unchanged optimized frame compare equal and expose the same current state; object identity across accesses need not be stable.

source_positions.section: Specification/Behavior of f_locals for optimized functions
source_positions.excerpt:
Behavior of f_locals for optimized functions
--------------------------------------------

Although ``f.f_locals`` behaves as if it were the namespace of the function, 
some differences will be observable, 
most notably that ``f.f_locals is f.f_locals`` may be ``False``.

However ``f.f_locals == f.f_locals`` will be ``True`` and
any changes to the underlying variables, by any means, will be
visible to all accesses to those variables.

whole_must.failure_condition: Equal frame state produces unequal mappings, or one retained view does not observe the change.

whole_must.predicate: A callable taking the single documentation string returns a runtime-checkable metadata object whose documentation attribute contains the exact same string.

source_positions.excerpt:
The main proposal is to have a new function ``doc()`` in the ``typing`` module.
Even though this is not strictly related to the type annotations, it's expected
to go in ``Annotated`` type annotations, and to interact with type annotations.

There's also the particular benefit that it could be implemented in the
``typing_extensions`` package to have support for older versions of Python and
early adopters of this proposal.

This ``doc()`` function would receive one single parameter ``documentation`` with
a documentation string.

This string could be a multi-line string, in which case, when extracted by tools,
should be interpreted cleaning up indentation as if using ``inspect.cleandoc()``,
the same procedure used for docstrings.

This string could probably contain markup, like Markdown or reST. As that could
be highly debated, that decision is left for a future proposal, to focus here
on the main functionality.

This specification targets static analysis tools and editors, and as such, the
value passed to ``doc()`` should allow static evaluation and analysis. If a
developer passes as the value something that requires runtime execution
(e.g. a function call) the behavior of static analysis tools is unspecified
and they could omit it from their process and results. For static analysis
tools to be conformant with this specification they need only to support
statically accessible values.

An example documenting the attributes of a class, or in this case, the keys
of a ``TypedDict``, could look like this:

.. code-block::

    from typing import Annotated, TypedDict, NotRequired, doc


    class User(TypedDict):
        firstname: Annotated[str, doc("The user's first name")]
        lastname: Annotated[str, doc("The user's last name")]


An example documenting the parameters of a function could look like this:

.. code-block::

    from typing import Annotated, doc


    def create_user(
        lastname: Annotated[str, doc("The **last name** of the newly created user")],
        firstname: Annotated[str | None, doc("The user's **first name**")] = None,
    ) -> Annotated[User, doc("The created user after saving in the database")]:
        """
        Create a new user in the system, it needs the database connection to be already
        initialized.
        """
        pass


The return of the ``doc()`` function is an instance of a class that can be checked
and used at runtime, defined as:

.. code-block::

    class DocInfo:
        def __init__(self, documentation: str):
            self.documentation = documentation

...where the attribute ``documentation`` contains the same value string passed to
the function ``doc()``.

source_positions.excerpt:
This proposal intends to address these shortcomings by extending and complementing the
information in docstrings, keeping backwards compatibility with existing docstrings,
and doing it in a way that leverages the Python language and structure, via type
annotations with ``Annotated``, and a new function in ``typing``.

The reason why this would belong in the standard Python library instead of an
external package is because although the implementation would be quite trivial,
the actual power and benefit from it would come from being a standard, so that
editors and other tools could implement support for it.

This doesn't deprecate current usage of docstrings, it's transparent to common
developers (library users), and it's only opt-in for library authors that would
like to adopt it.

whole_must.failure_condition: The mechanism removes/replaces the existing docstring or requires unrelated authors to adopt it.

source_positions.excerpt:
Nested ``Annotated``
--------------------

Continuing with the same idea above, if ``Annotated`` was used nested and used
multiple times in the same parameter, ``doc()`` would refer to the type it
is annotating.

So, in an example like:

.. code-block::

    def hi(
      to: Annotated[
            Annotated[str, doc("A user name")] | Annotated[list, doc("A list of user names")],
            doc("Who to say hi to"),
      ],
    ) -> None: ...


The documentation for the whole parameter ``to`` would be considered to be
"``Who to say hi to``".

The documentation for the case where that parameter ``to`` is specifically a ``str``
would be considered to be "``A user name``".

The documentation for the case where that parameter ``to`` is specifically a
``list`` would be considered to be "``A list of user names``".

Implementers would only be required to support the top level use case, where the

An example documenting the attributes of a class, or in this case, the keys

.. code-block::

    from typing import Annotated, TypedDict, NotRequired, doc


    class User(TypedDict):
        firstname: Annotated[str, doc("The user's first name")]
        lastname: Annotated[str, doc("The user's last name")]


An example documenting the parameters of a function could look like this:

.. code-block::

    from typing import Annotated, doc


    def create_user(
        lastname: Annotated[str, doc("The **last name** of the newly created user")],
        firstname: Annotated[str | None, doc("The user's **first name**")] = None,
    ) -> Annotated[User, doc("The created user after saving in the database")]:

        initialized.
        """

source_positions.excerpt:
This proposal intends to address these shortcomings by extending and complementing the
information in docstrings, keeping backwards compatibility with existing docstrings,
and doing it in a way that leverages the Python language and structure, via type
annotations with ``Annotated``, and a new function in ``typing``.

The reason why this would belong in the standard Python library instead of an
external package is because although the implementation would be quite trivial,
the actual power and benefit from it would come from being a standard, so that
editors and other tools could implement support for it.

This doesn't deprecate current usage of docstrings, it's transparent to common
developers (library users), and it's only opt-in for library authors that would
like to adopt it.

source_positions.excerpt:
Wheel Major Version Bump
------------------------

This PEP requires a wheel major version bump, so the ``Wheel-Version`` for wheels generated with
``LINKS`` **MUST** be at least version ``2.0``, so that older installers do not silently fail to
install symlinks and break user environments. For more see :pep:`777`.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Produce a wheel containing link metadata and inspect its Wheel-Version; present it to an installer limited to wheel 1.x.
whole_must.failure_condition: It declares a 1.x format or an older installer silently installs an incomplete package.

whole_must.predicate: The .dist-info/LINKS file represents source_path,target_path pairs within the wheel’s package/namespace roots, with the stated non-dangling target requirement.

source_positions.excerpt:
New ``LINKS`` Metadata File
---------------------------

To enable cross-platform symlinks, this PEP introduces a new wheel metadata file, ``LINKS``. An
example of a ``LINKS`` file is below::

    my_package/libfoo.so.3.1.4,my_package/libfoo.so.3
    my_package/libfoo.so.3,my_package/libfoo.so

The format of ``LINKS``, as can seen above, is ``source_path,target_path`` where ``source_path``
is a path relative to the root of any namespace or package root in the wheel. ``target_path`` is a
*non-dangling* path (i.e. a path that exists on the filesystem after the wheel's contents are
extracted) in a package or namespace of any package in the wheel. This means that if a wheel
contains multiple packages, all paths in packages in the wheel are acceptable.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Supply LINKS entries covering two package roots in one wheel plus a missing target.
whole_must.failure_condition: The metadata is not representable as the specified pairs or a dangling target is accepted. The first text’s example/prose orientation conflict remains unresolved.

whole_must.predicate: The installer resolves each path before validating that BOTH source and target remain within namespaces/packages coming from the wheel.

source_positions.excerpt:
Installers **MUST** resolve the paths of any link contained in the ``LINKS`` file *before*
deciding if any ``source_path`` or ``target_path`` are valid. Installers **MUST** verify that
``source_path`` and ``target_path`` are located inside any namespace or package coming from the
wheel.  Installers **MUST** reject cyclic symlinks in wheels. Installers **MAY** error if a long
chain of symlinks (symlinks pointing to symlinks many times repeated) exceeds a limit set by the
installer.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Use a path containing parent traversal or an already-existing symlink whose resolved destination is outside every package root supplied by the wheel.
whole_must.failure_condition: A lexical-prefix check accepts an escaping resolved path.

whole_must.predicate: The installer rejects cyclic link graphs and bounds depth checking to avoid unbounded cyclic/long-chain processing.

source_positions.excerpt:
In particular, the following checks **MUST** be made by installers:

1. That the symlinks do not point outside of any packages or namespaces coming from the wheel
2. That the symlinks are not dangling (the target exists at install time)
3. That the symlinks are not cyclical, stopping after a certain depth of checking to avoid denial
   of service requests

whole_must.falsifying_input: Provide A to B, B to A, and a chain exceeding the checker’s declared depth bound.
whole_must.failure_condition: A cycle is accepted or validation runs without a finite depth bound; no particular numeric limit is invented.

whole_must.predicate: Installation checks for LINKS, extracts ordinary package/data files first, and validates that every target exists in an extracted package namespace before link creation.

source_positions.excerpt:
Installers **MUST** follow the following steps when handling a wheel with symlinks:

1. Check for the existance of a ``LINKS`` file in the ``.dist-info``. If it does not exist,
   no further steps are required.
2. Extract all files in the wheel packages and data directory as in wheel 1.x.
3. Verify that for each ``source_path`` and ``target_path`` pairs, the ``target_path`` exists in
   one of the package namespaces just extracted.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Provide a wheel where one declared target is absent after extraction, alongside valid entries.
whole_must.failure_condition: The installer creates links without detecting the absent target or tries to use not-yet-extracted targets.

whole_must.predicate: The installer checks whether the current platform can create a suitable link for each file/folder pair and raises an error when it cannot.

source_positions.excerpt:
4. Next, check that the installer can make some kind of link for each pair in the site directory.
   If the installer cannot make a link for the file/folder ``target_path`` for the current
   platform, an error **MUST** be raised. An example of a failure mode would be a UNIX symlink to
   a file target, where the installer is running on Windows and the installer cannot make
   symlinks but can make junctions. In this case the installer **MUST** error because it cannot
   handle the link.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Request a file symlink on a platform where the installer can only create directory junctions.
whole_must.failure_condition: The unsupported file link is reported as successfully installed.

whole_must.predicate: For supported entries the installer creates a platform-relevant link and does not copy target content by default; copying may be an explicit alternate configuration only.

source_positions.excerpt:
5. Finally, the installer **MUST** add a platform-relevant link between ``source_path`` and
   ``target_path``.

Installers **MUST NOT** by default copy files instead of generating a symlink when handling
symlinks. Installers **MAY** have such behavior available under an alternate configuration or
command line flag.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Install a supported link with default options and inspect the result and disk-content duplication.
whole_must.failure_condition: The default silently copies the file instead of creating a link.

whole_must.predicate: Build backends apply the target’s inclusion decision to the symlink and verify that LINKS contains no dangling symlinks.

source_positions.excerpt:
Build Backend Specification
---------------------------

When creating a wheel, build backends **MUST** treat symlinks in the same way as its target when
deciding whether to include the symlink in a wheel. Build backends **MUST** verify that there are
no dangling symlinks in the ``LINKS`` file. Build backends **SHOULD** recognize platform-relevant
symlinks that would be included in builds. On Unix this is typically symlinks, on Windows this
includes symlinks and junctions.

whole_must.falsifying_input: Exclude a target from the build while a symlink to it is present, or include a symlink whose target is missing.
whole_must.failure_condition: The backend emits a dangling metadata entry or includes/excludes the symlink inconsistently with the target.

whole_must.predicate: Removal does not follow symlinks into their target contents.

3. That the symlinks are not cyclical, stopping after a certain depth of checking to avoid denial
   of service requests

Do not follow symlinks on removal.
